q1: SELECT name FROM drinker WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT f.bar FROM frequents AS f, serves AS s WHERE f.drinker = drinker.name AND f.bar = s.bar AND NOT s.beer IN (SELECT beer FROM likes WHERE drinker = drinker.name))
q2: WITH BarBeers AS (SELECT bar, beer FROM serves), DrinkerLikes AS (SELECT drinker, beer FROM likes), DrinkerFrequencies AS (SELECT DISTINCT drinker, bar FROM frequents) SELECT df.drinker FROM DrinkerFrequencies AS df LEFT JOIN BarBeers AS bb ON df.bar = bb.bar LEFT JOIN DrinkerLikes AS dl ON df.drinker = dl.drinker AND bb.beer = dl.beer GROUP BY df.drinker, df.bar HAVING COUNT(bb.beer) = COUNT(dl.beer) AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM serves AS s LEFT JOIN likes AS l ON s.beer = l.beer AND df.drinker = l.drinker WHERE s.bar = df.bar AND l.drinker IS NULL)

explanation: Q1 requires that for all bars a drinker frequents, all beers served at those bars are liked. Q2 returns a drinker if there exists at least one bar they frequent where all served beers are liked, even if other frequented bars have unliked beers. This difference arises because Q1 uses a global NOT EXISTS check across all bars, while Q2's HAVING clause per-bar grouping allows inclusion if any bar passes.
counterexample_dsp: A drinker (Alice) frequents two bars. Bar1 serves BeerA (liked by Alice), and Bar2 serves BeerB (not liked). Q1 excludes Alice because Bar2 has an unliked beer. Q2 includes Alice because Bar1 passes the per-bar check.
